**The last night**

My last night shift was Saturday, 7 November. I started at nine in the evening and finished at half past seven the next morning, in majors. Fourteen years of nights, beginning as an SHO in 2012, and then, just like that, the last one.

From Monday, I’ll be on the days-only rota. It’s the right decision. My knees have been making their feelings known; sleep has become less something I do than something I negotiate. And my GP has made it clear that my blood pressure is no longer a topic for jokes. I know all of that. I’m still surprised by how much I’m grieving.

I thought I’d write something about it months ago, when the change was first agreed. Every attempt came out either as a eulogy or a complaint. Neither seemed quite true. Nights weren’t a noble calling, and the NHS doesn’t need another late-night dispatch from me about what is wrong with it. I’ve written enough of those. This is about what the nights gave me, and what they asked in return.

People often think night work is all adrenaline: the sudden rush, the sharp decisions, the stories you tell afterwards. There is some of that. But most of a night is not a dramatic scene. It is a long stretch of small decisions, repeated under strange light. It is trying to keep your voice steady and your manner gentle when you are tired enough to feel your own patience thinning. It is staying kind at five in the morning, when you are empty.

The department feels different at night. Not better, exactly, and not easier. More itself, perhaps. There are fewer managers around and fewer layers between people. You see colleagues as they are when the day’s performance has fallen away: practical, funny, blunt, generous. Kindness is less likely to arrive with a grand gesture. It looks like someone noticing you haven’t sat down, or taking the next job without needing to be asked.

Our charge nurse, Folasade, has been doing nights for 22 years. She still beats me up the stairs. I have never quite decided whether to find this inspiring or irritating. Perhaps both. There is something reassuring about watching someone who knows exactly what she is doing, moving through a difficult shift without turning it into a performance. She is part of the department’s night-time grammar: steady, unshowy, already halfway up the stairs while the rest of us are considering whether we really need to go up them.

And then there is the toast.

At four in the morning, someone makes toast in the staff room. Always. Nobody admits to starting it. There is no rota, no conversation, no formal agreement. You can be halfway through a shift and suddenly the smell is there, warm and ordinary. Someone has put bread in the toaster. Someone else will appear. For a few minutes the night has a centre of gravity.

My first winter on nights, I cried in the car park at the Infirmary because I couldn’t remember whether I had given a second dose. I had. I checked, and I had. But I remember the uncertainty more clearly than the answer: the cold, the frost on the windscreen, the sense that I had somehow misplaced a piece of myself. It was one of those moments when you realise that being responsible does not mean being certain all the time. You have to check. You have to ask. You have to carry on, a little humbled.

Last winter, around three in the morning, an old gentleman held my hand and told me I had his daughter’s hands. I won’t say more about him. He went home three days later. I have thought about that sentence since, not because it was profound, but because it was so simple. For a moment, in the middle of a night that belonged to the hospital, there was something familiar between us. I was a person with hands, not just a doctor with a list of tasks. He was a person far from home, not just a patient in a bed. Then the shift went on.

There are things I missed. I watched both my nieces’ naming ceremonies over video because I was working nights. My sister never once complained. She was in Bangalore, making room for me in the family day from a distance; I was on the other side of a screen, trying to be present in the gaps between work and sleep. I am grateful she never made me feel guilty. I’m also sad that gratitude can’t give those mornings back.

The last shift itself was, in the end, a shift. There were patients to see, decisions to make, jobs to hand over. No ceremony, no pause in the work to mark the end of an era. I was glad of that. A last night doesn’t need to know it’s the last night. It can just be a night.

On Sunday morning I drove home down the London Road, the sun coming up. Radio 4’s shipping forecast was playing on catch-up. I realised that I would not see that particular light from this side again: the slow arrival of morning after a full night awake, the city appearing as if it had been quietly put back in place while I was elsewhere.

I felt relief. And then I felt like a traitor for feeling relieved.

I don’t think those feelings cancel each other out. You can love a part of your life and be ready to leave it. You can miss the people, the rhythms, the particular fellowship of an hour when the rest of the world is asleep, and still know that your body has had enough. Relief is not a verdict on the work or on the people who continue to do it. It is just the truth about what this work has cost me, alongside what it gave.

On Monday, I’ll wake up and go to work in daylight. I’m not sure yet what I’ll do with the extra mornings, or how long it will take for my sleep to believe that it is allowed to settle. I’ll miss the night shift’s strange closeness: the shared jokes that only make sense at four, the small kindnesses, the way people look after one another without making a speech about it.

Folasade will still be there, I expect, beating everyone up the stairs. And at four in the morning, someone will put bread in the toaster. They won’t admit to it. Someone else will come in, smell the toast, and stay for a minute.

I like to think that’s how it should be: the work continues, the kindness passes from one person to the next, and there is always, somehow, enough toast.
